Guidance

Apply for a seasonal river mooring permit

How to apply for a permit to keep a boat on a public river mooring for more than 14 days, what it costs, and what to do if your application is refused.

  • English
  • Tavensk
From:
Department for Rivers and Harbours
Published
14 January 2026
Last updated
2 September 2026 — See all updates
Applies to Upper Taven and the Marrow Isles

Contents

  1. Who needs a permit
  2. Types of permit
  3. Before you apply
  4. How to apply
  5. Fees
  6. After you apply

Who needs a permit

You need a seasonal mooring permit if you keep a boat on a public river mooring in Upper Taven or the Marrow Isles for more than 14 days in a row between 1 April and 31 October. The permit is issued for one named boat and one stretch of river, and it cannot be passed on to another owner.

You do not need a permit to stop overnight at a visitor mooring, to moor at a private marina, or to tie up on land you own. If you are not sure whether a mooring is public, check the register of public river moorings before you apply, because the application fee is not refunded when a permit turns out to be unnecessary.

The permit covers the boat, not the people aboard. If you live on the boat for the whole season you must also register it as a residential vessel, which is a separate process with its own safety inspection.

Types of permit

There are 3 types of permit, and the one you need depends on the length of your boat and on how long you intend to stay on the same stretch. You can hold only one permit for each boat at any time.

  • a standard permit, for boats up to 12 metres staying for the whole season
  • a short-stay permit, for boats of any length staying between 15 and 60 days
  • a large-vessel permit, for boats longer than 12 metres staying for the whole season

A short-stay permit can be extended once, for up to 30 days, if the harbour officer for your stretch agrees that there is room. You must ask for an extension at least 7 days before the permit runs out, and it is charged at the weekly rate shown in the table of fees.

Commercial operators, including hire fleets, trip boats and floating cafés, cannot use a seasonal mooring permit. They need a river trading licence, which sets its own conditions on waste, noise and opening hours.

Before you apply

Applications open on 15 January each year and are dealt with in the order they arrive. Popular stretches close to town quays fill within a few weeks, so it is worth choosing a stretch from the map of public mooring stretches and gathering your documents before the opening date.

You will need to send copies of the following documents with your application, and each one must be valid on the day the permit would start, not only on the day you apply:

  • the boat’s registration certificate, showing you as the owner or keeper
  • a boat safety certificate issued within the last 4 years
  • proof of third-party insurance for at least 2 million crowns
  • a photograph of the boat taken from the side, showing its name and registration number

If the boat is owned jointly, one owner should apply and list the others on the form. The department will write only to the applicant, and that person is responsible for making sure the conditions of the permit are met for the whole season.

You cannot apply for a stretch that is marked on the map as closed for bank repairs. The list of closed stretches is updated on the first working day of every month.

How to apply

The quickest way to apply is online. Most online applications are decided within 10 working days, and you can save a partly completed form and return to it later, as long as you finish it within 28 days.

Apply for a mooring permit online. You will need a Taven Sign-In account, which you can create when you start.

Whichever way you apply, the process is the same, and it helps to know the order of the steps before you begin, because a missing document is the most common reason for a delay:

  1. Choose the stretch of river and the type of permit you want.

  2. Fill in the application form and attach copies of your documents.

  3. Pay the application fee. Your application is not complete until the payment has cleared.

  4. Wait for the harbour officer’s decision, which is sent by email or by post, depending on what you chose on the form.

  5. Fix the permit disc to the boat, where it can be read from the bank, before you moor.

If you cannot apply online, you can ask for a paper form by writing to the Mooring Permit Team at the address at the end of this guidance. Paper applications take longer, usually around 25 working days, and they must be paid for by cheque or bank transfer.

You can also email the team at mooring.permits@drh.gov.taven.example if you need the form in large print, in braille or in another language. Tell them which format you need and where to send it.

Fees

The fee has 2 parts: an application fee, which pays for checking your documents, and a seasonal charge based on the length of the boat. The application fee is kept even if the permit is refused or you withdraw, but the seasonal charge is refunded in full.

Type of fee Who pays it Amount
Application fee All applicants 38 crowns
Standard permit Boats up to 8 metres 310 crowns
Standard permit Boats over 8 metres and up to 12 metres 425 crowns
Large-vessel permit Boats over 12 metres 640 crowns
Short-stay permit Any boat, for each week 29 crowns
Replacement permit disc Holders who lose a disc 12 crowns

You can pay by debit card, by credit card or by bank transfer. If you receive the Low Income Boaters’ Allowance, the seasonal charge is halved, and you should enter your allowance reference on the form so that the reduction is applied before you pay.

Fees are reviewed every year and the new rates are published in December. A permit is charged at the rate in force on the day the application is received, even if the season it covers begins after the rates have changed.

After you apply

If your application is approved, you will be sent a permit disc and a letter that sets out the conditions for your stretch. The disc must be displayed on the side of the boat facing the bank from the first day of mooring, and a harbour officer may ask to see the letter.

While the permit is in force you must keep to its conditions. A harbour officer can cancel a permit without a refund if the holder, or anyone using the boat with their agreement, does any of the following:

  • moors outside the stretch named on the permit for more than 48 hours
  • runs an engine or generator between 10pm and 7am
  • blocks the towpath or a slipway with ropes, gangplanks or stored belongings
  • empties waste tanks anywhere other than a pump-out station

If your application is refused, the letter will give the reason. The most common reasons are that the stretch is full, that a document has expired, or that the boat is too long for the mooring. You can apply again for a different stretch in the same season without paying a second application fee.

You can ask for a refusal or a cancellation to be reviewed by someone who was not involved in the first decision. Write to the review officer within 21 days of the date on the letter, explain why you think the decision was wrong, and include your application reference.

Mooring Permit Reviews

Wharf House

Harrowmere

Reviews are usually completed within 15 working days. If you are still unhappy after the review, you can take the matter to the Waterways Adjudicator, an independent body that does not charge for looking at complaints about permits.
